events.title: A phishing email opens the door
events.headline: The entire crisis began with a single unopened suspicion: one clerk, one invoice, one macro
events.body: On the evening before Thanksgiving, a supplier-onboarding clerk at Maison Aubray's head office received an email that looked like a routine invoice from a prospective supplier. The attachment was a booby-trapped spreadsheet: opening it and enabling the macro silently installed a first-stage loader on the clerk's workstation. No EDR alert fired, and the clerk, finishing a backlog of Black Friday supplier files, noticed nothing. The intrusion group later calling itself VEIL-9 had just gained their foothold, timed deliberately ahead of the year's busiest retail weekend.

events.title: The attacker establishes a silent foothold
events.headline: Within 24 hours, the intruders had a permanent channel — and nobody knew they were inside
events.body: The loader beaconed out and downloaded a remote-access tool, giving VEIL-9 operators interactive control. They established persistence on two workstations, configured the beacon to blend in with normal administrative traffic, and spent the day simply watching: mapping the network, reading the clerk's mailbox, identifying the head-office domain structure. There was no encryption, no theft, no noise — just reconnaissance. The lack of any detection here meant the intruders would enjoy three uninterrupted weeks of freedom inside the network.
artifacts: C2 traffic blended with admin protocols

events.title: Stolen credentials unlock the heart of the domain
events.headline: A weak service account password turned a workspace compromise into total control of the IT estate
events.body: The attackers ran Kerberoasting attacks against service accounts and cracked the password of a backup service account — a highly privileged account with read access to nearly everything. Using it, they moved laterally from the workstation tier to the domain controllers, effectively becoming administrators of the entire Maison Aubray IT environment. From the domain controllers they enumerated the backup infrastructure, the e-commerce build pipeline, the hypervisor estate at head office and the two logistics hubs. At this point, nothing could stop them except discovery — and no one discovered them.
artifacts: Lateral movement logs to domain controllers

events.title: A card skimmer is injected into the online checkout
events.headline: Long before the ransomware detonated, customers' card data was already being stolen during checkout
events.body: From their foothold, the attackers reached the e-commerce build pipeline and injected a short piece of JavaScript into the checkout page bundle. The skimmer activated only for a subset of card payments, silently copying card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs as customers typed them, and POSTing them to an attacker-controlled domain. During the ten days before detonation — including early Black Friday traffic — thousands of transactions were skimmed. This quiet monetization channel ran in parallel to the ransomware preparation and was invisible to everyone until fraud patterns surfaced on crisis day.
artifacts: Unknown external domain receiving POST data
events.damageUSD: Early fraud exposure on skimmed cards: est. several hundred thousand euros

events.title: 1.8 terabytes of data exfiltrated
events.headline: The ransom demand was never really about decryption — the leverage was stolen data, copied long before the deadline
events.body: Using the backup service account's broad read rights, VEIL-9 staged and exfiltrated approximately 1.8 TB of data to cloud storage they controlled: the full customer database of 6 million loyalty-card accounts (names, emails, phone numbers, purchase histories, partial payment metadata), HR files on 18,000 employees, and supplier contracts. The exfiltration ran overnight at throttled speeds to avoid bandwidth alerts. This theft is what transformed a ransomware incident into a double-extortion case with hard GDPR obligations, and it was complete six days before anyone suspected anything.
artifacts: 1.8 TB staged and pushed to external cloud storage

events.title: Backups are sabotaged in silence
events.headline: The attackers spent two days ensuring recovery would be as painful as possible — while everything still looked normal
events.body: Two days before detonation, VEIL-9 used the backup service account to delete backup catalogues and reduce snapshot retention to zero across the backup platform. The last viable, clean backup of the ERP, warehouse management system and file shares was effectively eliminated. On the surface, Thursday before Black Friday was a completely normal peak-preparation day at head office. In reality, the recovery strategy the company thought it could rely on had already been dismantled.

events.title: Ransomware detonates across head office and logistics
events.headline: At 05:50 on the biggest retail morning of the year, the company's digital nervous system stopped
events.body: Minutes before warehouse shifts began and hours before 420 stores opened, VEIL-9 deployed ransomware simultaneously across the hypervisors of the head office and both logistics hubs. Every virtual machine died at once: ERP, warehouse management, store back-office, file shares, intranet. A ransom note appeared on every screen. Replenishment, pricing updates, loyalty processing and e-commerce fulfilment all froze. The attackers had deliberately timed detonation for the moment it would hurt most — Black Friday, with no clean backups and stolen data already in hand.
artifacts: Simultaneous encryption timestamps across two sites
events.casualties: ERP, WMS, store back-office, file shares and intranet all offline
events.damageUSD: Peak-day revenue at risk: est. 4-5% of annual sales

events.title: 420 stores open blind in degraded mode
events.headline: With no price files, no loyalty and no back-office, the entire physical retail network carried on by improvising
events.body: By 06:30, store back-office servers were unreachable and every store learned it was on its own. Managers fell back on printed price lists and standalone payment terminals that still worked offline. Checkout queues lengthened, loyalty points couldn't be applied, and cash handling rules loosened under pressure. Regional store networks organized themselves over WhatsApp groups — an informal coordination channel that became the company's de facto operational lifeline, and later a communication risk. For most store staff, this was the first visible sign that something was badly wrong.
events.casualties: 420 stores trading without price files, loyalty or stock visibility

events.title: Forensics reveals a weeks-old intrusion and dead backups
events.headline: The IR team's first readout changed everything: this was not a fresh attack, and recovery assumptions were wrong
events.body: The engaged incident response team's preliminary forensic findings overturned the crisis cell's starting assumptions. The encryption was not a fast overnight hit — the attackers had been inside for over three weeks, obtained domain admin via Kerberoasting of a backup service account, and had systematically destroyed the backups two days before detonating. The implication was immediate and grave: the stolen data threat was credible, the exfiltration window was long, and rebuilding from recent backups was not an option. The recovery plan had to be rewritten mid-crisis.

events.title: VEIL-9 demands 12 million euros
events.headline: At 09:30, extortion became personal: a direct ransom email to the CEO with a 72-hour clock
events.body: The attackers emailed the CEO directly, claiming credit for the outage and demanding €12,000,000 within 72 hours. The demand was explicit: pay or the stolen customer database would be published, and — worse — the group claimed to hold 'card data' from the online shop, implying the payment channel itself was compromised. This claim was initially treated as possible bluff, since it was technically hard to verify quickly. It also placed the ransom decision squarely on the executive committee's desk, with legal, regulatory and negotiation dimensions colliding with the ongoing technical response.
artifacts: Claims of customer and card data possession

events.title: The checkout skimmer is confirmed
events.headline: VEIL-9's 'card data' claim was not a bluff: the online checkout had been harvesting customers' cards for ten days
events.body: SOC analysis of the checkout page confirmed the anomaly: a JavaScript file loaded from a non-whitelisted external domain was capturing card data as customers typed it and POSTing it to attacker infrastructure. The skimmer had been live since D-10, meaning every skimmed transaction during the pre-Black Friday run-up was compromised. The executive committee now faced an excruciating dilemma on the busiest sales day of the year: isolate e-commerce and stop the bleeding at massive revenue cost, or leave it up and risk further card theft. The decision could not wait for forensic completeness.
artifacts: Confirmed skimmer script POSTing to attacker domain
events.damageUSD: Card reissuance and fraud liability exposure: est. several million euros

events.title: Customer data sample published on the leak site
events.headline: The threat became real at 10:15: a sample of real customer records appeared online as proof
events.body: Just before 10:15, VEIL-9 published a sample of the stolen data on their leak site as a pressure tactic, alongside a full inventory of what they claimed to hold: 6 million loyalty accounts, HR files and corporate contracts. The leak was picked up on social media within minutes, spread through the Black Friday online conversation, and reached the press. The company's decision window on proactive communication and GDPR notification effectively closed: the breach was now public knowledge before the company had notified its customers or completed its own assessment.
artifacts: Customer data sample on leak site

events.title: The acquiring bank confirms the fraud pattern
events.headline: Independent external evidence confirmed the payment breach: the acquiring bank traced card fraud back to the Aubray checkout
events.body: At 10:40, the acquiring bank's fraud monitoring identified a clear common point of purchase pattern: a cluster of fraudulent card transactions whose only shared merchant was Maison Aubray's online shop. The bank alerted the CEO and CISO, imposed PCI DSS forensic preservation requirements — forbidding the rebuilding or wiping of compromised systems — and signalled that card brand escalation, potential fines and, in the worst case, loss of card acceptance were now on the table. The payment chain compromise was no longer an internal suspicion: it was externally corroborated fact.
artifacts: Common point of purchase fraud analysis
Acquiring bank alerts to CEO and CISO
events.damageUSD: PCI fines and fraud liability: est. €1-3M exposure

events.title: The committee locks in its core decisions under media fire
events.headline: By late morning, four cells needed one coherent answer on e-commerce, payments, ransom and communication
events.body: Under simultaneous pressure — a leaking customer-data story, a national TV breaking-news banner, a call centre at eight times normal volume, stores demanding a firm card-payment instruction before the lunch rush, and employees with no internal messaging — the crisis committee had to lock its arbitrations. The practical options were laid out: isolate e-commerce to stop skimming at severe Black Friday revenue cost, or keep selling with containment; take card payments in stores or go cash-only with the fraud and queueing consequences; hold a firm no-negotiation ransom stance while managing the 72-hour deadline; and launch GDPR Article 33 notification on the strength of confirmed exfiltration and public leak. Whatever each cell decided, the decisions had to be consistent, logged, and executable within the hour.
events.casualties: Call centre at 8x volume; employee channels overwhelmed

events.title: Notification, containment and the ransom clock run out
events.headline: The 72-hour deadline and the GDPR clock ran in parallel — both had to be managed deliberately, not reactively
events.body: Over the following 72 hours, the company filed its formal GDPR personal data breach notification covering the 6 million affected loyalty accounts, notified the cyber authority under NIS2 obligations as an essential/large retail operator, and cooperated with the acquiring bank's forensic process while keeping the compromised checkout isolated. On the ransom, the executive line held against payment: the demand was referred to law enforcement, negotiation was not initiated, and the company prepared for a full data leak instead — communicating to customers with breach notifications, credit-monitoring offers and card-reissuance coordination with the banks. VEIL-9 partially published more data when the deadline passed, as anticipated.
artifacts: Law enforcement referral of the ransom demand
events.damageUSD: Regulatory exposure: GDPR fines up to 4% of turnover (€124M theoretical maximum)

events.title: Rebuilding without backups
events.headline: Because the backup sabotage succeeded, recovery meant rebuilding from near zero — weeks, not days
events.body: With recent backups unrecoverable, IT rebuilt the hypervisor estate, ERP and warehouse management from older offline archives and vendor media, restoring in priority order: payments and store back-office first, then e-commerce (rebuilt clean, with the skimmer's injection vector — the build pipeline — hardened with signed commits and access controls), then ERP and WMS. Stores traded in degraded mode for roughly ten days; full e-commerce resumed in week two after a clean rebuild and a PCI forensic sign-off. Estimated combined costs — lost Black Friday revenue, incident response, rebuilding, notification, card reissuance and legal — ran to the tens of millions of euros, before any regulatory fine.
artifacts: PCI forensic sign-off before checkout relaunch
events.damageUSD: Est. €25-40M total incident cost before fines

events.title: Root causes: phishing, a weak service account and invisible exfiltration
events.headline: The final review traced the whole chain: three weeks of dwell time, three failures that let it happen
events.body: The post-incident review identified the causal chain. First, a phishing email reached a clerk and a malicious macro executed — no effective email sandboxing or endpoint hardening. Second, a weak, over-privileged backup service account allowed Kerberoasting and domain-wide compromise — the same account that both enabled the 1.8 TB theft and let the attackers destroy the backups. Third, neither the two-week intrusion, the skimmer injection, nor the massive exfiltration triggered any alert — monitoring covered the perimeter but not internal east-west traffic, backup changes or build-pipeline integrity. The remediation plan: phishing-resistant authentication and macro blocking, removal of over-privileged service accounts, immutable and logically isolated backups, e-commerce supply-chain integrity checks, and detection tuned to backup tampering and lateral movement. The lesson: the crisis of Black Friday morning was not made that morning — it was made in the three silent weeks before it.

slide_debrief.key_messages:
The exercise stressed all four cells with simultaneous ransomware, suspected card skimming, GDPR 72-hour, PCI and NIS2 duties on the peak sales day.
The core arbitrations — isolate e-commerce, engage/stall/refuse the 12M€ ransom, notify without premature disclosure — had to be locked in by 10:40 when the acquiring bank forced the decision.
Evaluator marks are not yet recorded; the findings below are based on the exercise design and must be confirmed with participants during the hot wash.
Key learning objectives tested: one shared situation picture across four cells, a maintained decision log, and decisions made under uncertainty.
slide_debrief.went_well:
To be confirmed with participants; observed plausibly: the crisis cell convened at 08:00 as the procedure requires and established a first shared situation picture.
The four-cell structure was activated and each cell engaged its specific duties (forensics, holding statements, GDPR/PCI assessment, degraded store operations).
The scenario injected realistic pressure points (leak site, viral fraud post, bank ultimatum) that drove cross-cell coordination.
slide_debrief.to_improve:
Confirm in the hot wash whether the isolation decision for e-commerce and payment terminals was made proactively or only after the bank's ultimatum at 10:40.
Confirm whether the ransom decision framework (engage/stall/refuse) was discussed with legal constraints before the 72-hour deadline pressure built.
Confirm whether the GDPR 72-hour clock was formally started at 08:44 when exfiltration was confirmed, and whether the notification set was complete.
Confirm whether one consistent situation picture was actually shared across all four cells, or whether cells worked in silos.
Confirm whether decision logs were kept in real time in every cell, and whether communication stayed legally consistent after the leak went public.
slide_debrief.recommendations:
CISO to predefine a payment-isolation decision tree (e-commerce + terminals) with thresholds that do not wait for bank pressure — within 3 months.
Executive committee to adopt a written ransom decision framework (legal, insurance, sanctions, sanctions screening) validated by legal — within 3 months.
DPO to map the GDPR/PCI/NIS2 notification checklist with owners and deadlines, tested annually — within 2 months.
Crisis manager to formalise a cross-cell situation report cycle and mandatory decision-log template — within 1 month.
Head of customer service to size a customer-service surge plan for Black Friday-level social media pressure — within 3 months.
slide_debrief.next_steps:
Facilitators to collect evaluator marks and cell notes and issue the final after-action review within two weeks.
Hold the hot wash with all four cells to confirm the open questions above, especially the isolation and ransom decision timings.
Schedule a follow-up tabletop within six months focusing on the weakest criteria identified in the confirmed evaluation.
Integrate agreed actions into the group's crisis plan and next cyber resilience programme cycle.

result.summary: The chronogram delivers a coherent, well-paced ransomware + data theft + payment fraud scenario with a clear escalation arc and a strong final forced decision. Thematic coverage is good on IT, legal, communication and business continuity, but HR/social, suppliers/partners, insurance and ANSSI/NIS2 dimensions are weak or absent despite stated objectives. Metadata is complete for all 33 stimuli, but no conditional injects, nudges or reframing mechanisms are documented, which limits facilitator flexibility. Overall the design is an advanced draft requiring enriched themes and a contingency plan before play.

axes.title: Exercise Completeness
positive: Strong operational/technical coverage through IT & cyber injects (#01, #04, #07, #08, #16, #21, #23, #30)
Legal/regulatory dimension well represented with DPA (#19, #27), police (#10) and card scheme/PCI through the bank (#29, #30)
External communication covered via journalist, viral posts, TV and social media (#06, #12, #13, #20, #24, #25, #28)
Business continuity / degraded mode is a central thread (#03, #14, #31)
Ransom dilemma, CFO/insurance question (#22) and executive pressure (#18) test financial dimension
negative: HR/social dimension absent: no inject on employee anxiety, works council or HR data impact despite HR files being exfiltrated (incident timeline D-6) - employees only appear via Marc Delaunay (#05, #18, #32)
No ANSSI/NIS2 stimulus despite an explicit learning objective for the legal cell
No suppliers/partners stimulus although the initial access came through supplier onboarding - supplier chain and contract stakeholders are ignored
No inject explicitly requesting deliverables such as a press release, regulatory notification draft or structured sitrep from the cells
Channel diversity skewed: ~24 of 33 stimuli are email; only limited use of call, alert, social, TV and dark web
No BCP/DRP activation decision stimulus - degraded mode is stated as fact, never decided
recommendations: Add an HR/works council inject in Phase 3 or 4 (e.g., HR data detected in the leak sample, employee questions on payslips)
Add an ANSSI/NIS2 authority stimulus in Phase 2 or 3 to test the legal cell's notification obligations
Add a supplier or logistics partner inject (e.g., warehouse partner unable to receive orders, supplier contracts found in the leak)
Insert deliverable-forcing injects: request a holding statement by a deadline, a draft GDPR notification, and a 15-minute sitrep
Rebalance channels: replace 4-5 email injects with phone calls, a conference bridge or a media monitoring alert

axes.title: Narrative Coherence
positive: Clear five-phase structure with logical progression: alert (#01-#06), investigation and dilemma (#07-#14), ransom (#15-#22), public leak (#23-#28), forced decision (#29-#33)
Causal chaining is tight: skimmer suspicion (#08) → confirmation (#21) → bank fraud pattern (#29)
Severity escalation is gradual and credible (encryption → exfiltration → ransom → leak → bank ultimatum)
Scenario includes a genuine decision dilemma (#11: isolate e-commerce vs keep Black Friday sales), a twist (#29 bank forces the arbitration) and uncertainty phases (#07-#14)
Factual elements consistent: 1.8 TB exfiltration (#09) matches the leak (#23), ransom timing matches narrative arc
negative: Detection/early warning phase is absent: play starts at encryption with a recap (#01-#03), skipping the SOC escalation and on-call decision described in the incident timeline
3-hour duration is short for testing GDPR 72h notification and ransom 72h deadline - closure (#33) arrives before consequences of decisions can be felt
No stabilization/recovery or demobilization phase; the scenario ends at peak pressure without a wind-down
recommendations: Either accept the hot-phase scope explicitly or add a compressed 'T+24h' epilogue phase (recovery priorities, first notification status)
Consider a short pre-brief recap to compensate for the missing detection phase, or start one stimulus earlier with the SOC escalation

axes.title: Stimulus Coherence
positive: All 33 stimuli have complete metadata: timestamp, sender, recipient, channel, type
Propagation delays are realistic: forensic findings at H+0:33 after a 05:50 encryption, bank fraud report only after sufficient transaction volume (#29)
No factual contradictions detected between stimuli; exfiltration, ransom amount and leak content are consistent
negative: No Conditional column: injects such as #29 (bank forcing) should depend on whether players already isolated e-commerce, but this dependency is not marked
Inject #19 (DPA acknowledges contact) arrives at H+1:50 although no prior stimulus shows the legal cell contacting the DPA - assumes a player action without a conditional marker
Inject #27 states the regulator was 'reactively informed by press' - if players already notified (per #19), this framing contradicts their action; needs a conditional variant
recommendations: Introduce a Conditional column and mark at least #19, #27 and #29 as decision-dependent
Prepare two variants of #19/#27: one if the players notified the DPA proactively, one if they did not
Add a fallback inject if players isolate e-commerce before H+1:30 (e.g., bank acknowledges quick action, but sales-loss pressure escalates)

axes.title: Pace and Workload Per Cell
positive: No peaks exceeding 3 stimuli in 5 minutes for any cell; the maximum density is 2 stimuli in 6 minutes (Communication cell #24/#25)
Pace includes natural accelerations (Phase 4, six injects in 19 minutes) and breathers (Phase 3 spreads injects 4-8 minutes apart)
Every cell receives at least one stimulus in every phase, ensuring no cell is idle for a full phase
negative: Communication cell has a 30-minute gap between #25 (H+2:23) and #32 (H+2:53) precisely during the peak leak crisis - the cell under most pressure goes quiet
Strategic crisis cell has a 21-minute gap between #22 (H+2:04) and #28 (H+2:35) during which the leak breaks without a decision-forcing stimulus
Legal cell workload is heaviest (9 stimuli) while the decision dilemma mainly weighs on the strategic cell (8 stimuli) - imbalance may overload legal players
recommendations: Insert one communication-cell stimulus around H+2:40 (e.g., press office call volume or a competitor/influencer comment) to fill the gap
Add a strategic-cell stimulus between H+2:10 and H+2:35 asking for an interim position on the leak
Consider shifting one legal inject (#26 customer service) to the strategic cell to balance workload

axes.title: Contingency Management and Flexibility
positive: The linear chronogram is well sequenced enough that facilitators can anticipate the main decision points (#11, #15, #29)
Final inject #33 provides a natural synchronization point that can serve as an early-closure anchor
negative: No alternative injects are documented if players decide quickly (e.g., isolate e-commerce at H+0:50) or refuse to engage with the ransom
No nudge mechanism exists for a cell that stalls (e.g., legal cell failing to start the GDPR notification, IT cell not preserving evidence)
No reframing stimuli planned to bring play back on track if players take an unexpected direction (e.g., paying the ransom, contacting the attacker, shutting all stores)
No early stop mechanism is defined; the only endpoint is #33 at H+2:56
The missing Conditional column compounds the problem: dependencies on player actions are implicit and undocumented
recommendations: Create a contingency annex with 5-8 alternative injects keyed to the major decision points (early isolation, ransom engagement, refusal, notification to authorities)
Define nudge stimuli per cell (e.g., IR provider reminder about evidence preservation, DPO reminding the 72h clock)
Prepare reframing injects for likely off-script moves: negotiation with the attacker, premature public disclosure, full store closure
Document an early stop mechanism (facilitator criteria and a closing inject template) allowing closure at any phase boundary with a debrief trigger

priority_actions: Add a Conditional column and mark decision-dependent injects (#19, #27, #29) with alternative variants
Build a contingency annex: nudge injects per cell, reframing injects for off-script decisions, and an early stop mechanism
Close thematic gaps: add HR/works council, ANSSI/NIS2 and supplier/partner stimuli, plus deliverable-forcing injects (press release, sitrep, GDPR draft)
Fill the communication cell's 30-minute gap at H+2:23-H+2:53 and add a strategic-cell stimulus during the leak phase
Decide on the detection/early-warning and closure question: add a SOC escalation prelude and/or a T+24h epilogue, or explicitly document the hot-phase scope

review.summary: A coherent triple-extortion storyline follows the attack path faithfully and distributes dilemmas well, but the exercise ends abruptly with no recovery, crisis-exit or lessons-learned phase, several objectives (NIS2/ANSSI, ransom decision closure, GDPR notification drafting) are never forced to a decision, and a few sender-role inconsistencies and stress mismatches weaken realism. Rhythm is mostly good outside the two known dead zones.

issues.message: The play ends at H+2:56 inside 'The bank forces the decision' (containment, H+2:40) with no eradication, recovery, continuity or crisis-exit block. Objectives on recovery priorities and 'crisis exit' are never tested: the ransom stance, GDPR notification, terminal policy and customer messaging all remain open at freeze.
issues.suggestion: Add a short exit block (H+2:56–H+3:00) or convert the final phase's tail into an exit block: a decision-log consolidation inject, a draft GDPR notification request to the legal cell, and a 'state of play at 12:00' summary forcing each cell to lock its next steps.

issues.message: The ransom decision is never forced: after the demand at H+1:30 and the CFO constraints at H+2:10, the attacker's 72-hour clock produces no follow-up (no second contact, no countdown reminder, no partial-publication threat). The 'engage, stall, refuse' objective stays untested at decision level.
issues.suggestion: Add one inject at ~H+2:25 (e.g. VEIL-9 follow-up or dark-web countdown update to the strategic cell) forcing a logged ransom stance before the bank alert arrives, so the isolation arbitration is made with the ransom position already on the table.

issues.message: The journalist deadline inject at H+1:58 ('we will run the ransom story at 10:30') has no payoff: no article_press inject lands before the leak sample goes public at H+2:16, so the deadline threat evaporates. This breaks the media-cycle realism and wastes a good pressure moment.
issues.suggestion: Insert an article_press inject at ~H+2:12 (template lemonde or ft) to the Communication cell: 'Ransomware hits Aubray on Black Friday', between the deadline and the leak, so comms must react to the actual article before the viral posts.

issues.message: NIS2/ANSSI obligations are named in the objectives and the attack path, but no ANSSI inject exists anywhere: only the Cybercrime Unit (H+0:50) and the Data Protection Authority (H+1:50, H+2:31) contact the legal cell. The 24-hour early-warning duty is never tested.
issues.suggestion: Add one email_authority inject from ANSSI (or a NIS2 supervisory authority) around H+1:15–H+1:25 asking whether an early warning has been filed, before the DPA exchanges, so the two regulatory tracks (NIS2 24h vs GDPR 72h) compete for the legal cell.

issues.message: Sender-role inconsistencies: 'CFO: can we even pay?' at H+2:10 is sent by Pascal Rivet, the on-call IT manager (no CFO exists in the cast); 'Board and family shareholders pressing for answers' at H+1:44 and 'Customer service overwhelmed: call volumes x8' at H+2:27 both come from Marc Delaunay, the HR director, whose plausible remit is neither. Players will notice and it erodes immersion.
issues.suggestion: Re-source the CFO inject as an internal_memo from the finance direction (add a CFO cast member or generic sender), and route the customer-service surge inject through a customer service or store operations sender (e.g. Yvonne Lecoq or a new customer service director).

issues.message: Stress labels are misaligned with content: 'The leak goes public' (H+2:15–H+2:40) carries a viral fraud post, press amplification, a regulator demanding notification today and breaking TV news, yet is rated Tension — lower than the preceding twist phase; and 'The bank forces the decision' (Peak-level decision moment) is rated High, making the curve sag exactly when it should peak at the end.
issues.suggestion: Rate 'The leak goes public' as High or Peak and 'The bank forces the decision' as Peak, so the pressure curve rises monotonically to the final arbitration.

issues.message: The strategic crisis cell has a 25-minute silence between H+2:10 and H+2:35 (TV news), then three injects in 21 minutes at the very end while it must take the hardest decision of the exercise. During the leak storm it receives nothing to arbitrate.
issues.suggestion: Move one decision-oriented inject into the leak window (e.g. an e-commerce revenue/loss figure or a partner asking whether to suspend the loyalty programme at ~H+2:20), and keep the end-of-play sync but move it to H+2:58 to avoid stacking 3 injects on the decision cell in the final 20 minutes.

issues.message: The 'payment terminals' half of the core dilemma is under-motivated: the web skimmer only compromises the online checkout, yet injects at H+2:49 and the brief treat physical store terminals as part of the isolation decision. Standalone in-store terminals are not plausibly compromised by a checkout-page skimmer, weakening the realism of the arbitration.
issues.suggestion: Either scope the bank's demand and the store question to the online payment flow only, or add one earlier inject (e.g. in 'Scope, skimmer and the first arbitration') showing back-office/terminal-management servers were on the encrypted estate, justifying store-terminal doubt.

issues.message: The Communication cell never produces or receives a press release artifact across the whole play, despite the learning objective on holding statements: journalist contacts (H+0:22, H+1:14, H+1:58) all go to other cells or arrive as pressure, and the only comms outputs requested are an internal memo (H+2:53) and implicit responses.
issues.suggestion: Add one press_release-channel inject around H+2:36–H+2:40 (e.g. the CEO's office asking comms to publish the statement now that TV has broken the story) so the holding-statement objective has a concrete deliverable.

issues.message: The GDPR notification is never drafted or filed: the regulator 'expects notification today' at H+2:31, but no inject asks the legal cell to produce the notification or a reasoned deferral before freeze at H+2:56. The 72-hour clock is discussed but the deliverable is untested.
issues.suggestion: In the final block, add an inject to the legal cell at ~H+2:46: 'Draft the notification content or document the deferral rationale for the decision log', making the objective's output explicit.

issues.message: The IT & cyber cell's evidence-preservation thread is opened (Sentinelle CERT at H+0:14, police at H+0:50, bank forensics at H+2:45) but never receives a conflicting-action dilemma, e.g. pressure to wipe-and-rebuild the e-commerce server to restore sales before the leak vs preserving the skimmer evidence.
issues.suggestion: Add one inject at ~H+2:20 from e-commerce operations to the IT cell: 'Marketing demands we redeploy the checkout now', creating the evidence-vs-recovery conflict the forensics objective implies.

issues.message: The trigger phase front-loads six injects across four cells within 22 minutes with all major findings (ERP, WMS, backups down) delivered in the SOC alert, leaving little for players to discover and compressing the ambiguity the narrative promises.
issues.suggestion: Trim detail from the H+0:02 SOC alert (keep encryption, defer backup status) and let the 'backups unreachable' finding surface in 'Scope, skimmer and the first arbitration' to preserve early ambiguity.
